sentences.text: The holotype skeleton of Epidexipteryx hui measures 25 cm in length and was estimated to weigh 164 grams.
Its total length, including incomplete tail feathers, reached 44.5 cm.
The fossil includes four long tail feathers composed of a central rachis and vanes.
Unlike modern tail feathers, the vanes were made of a single ribbon-like sheet rather than individual branched filaments.
The tail vertebrae resembled the pygostyle found in modern birds and some oviraptorosaurs.
The skull resembles those of Sapeornis, oviraptorosaurs, and therizinosauroids.
Teeth were present only at the front of the jaws, with long forward-angled teeth projecting outward.
The hip configuration featured a pubis shorter than the ischium, a trait similar to Scansoriopteryx.
The body was covered in simpler feathers made of parallel scales similar to those of more primitive feathered dinosaurs.
Some body feathers appeared to have a unique membranous structure.
It is the earliest known dinosaur genus with ornamental feathers in the fossil record.
The fossil was found in the Daohugou Formation of Inner Mongolia, dating to approximately 168 to 160 million years ago.
The formal description was published in the journal Nature on October 23, 2008.
The species name Epidexipteryx hui honors paleomammologist Hu Yaoming, whose name means "Hu's display feather" in English and "Hu Yaoming's display dragon" in Chinese.
Researchers hypothesize that Epidexipteryx likely lacked wing feathers but may have had a membrane wing for gliding, similar to the related dinosaur Yi.
Scientists have suggested that the animal used its long claws to dig for grubs in trees, similar to the aye-aye.
Epidexipteryx belongs to the parent group Paraves.
The genus is classified within the class Reptilia.
The authors of its description recovered Epidexipteryx as a member of the family Scansoriopterygidae and as a basal member of the clade Avialae.
A separate exploratory analysis recovered Scansoriopteryx and Epidendrosaurus as basal Avialae members unrelated to Epidexipteryx, which remained outside Eumaniraptora.
A 2024 study by Cau suggests Epidexipteryx may be a junior synonym of Epidendrosaurus due to incomplete fossil evidence and variable traits.
It lived during the Callovian stage, from 165.3 to 161.5 million years ago.
Zhang et al. suggest that unless Epidexipteryx evolved from flying ancestors that later lost their wings, its advanced display tail feathers may have preceded flight or gliding.
